Jenna faltered. Just slightly. Just for a moment. The idea of donating money to Valphine's operation had reached her face before she could stop it.

"Torture cult," she said, or close to it.

"Torture cult!" Vukradin objected.

Then: "It is kind of a torture cult."

I said: "It kind of is."

Vukradin corrected this with care. "It's more like a masochism cult."

I considered it. Freedom of worship is a thing Vukradin has explained to me. Valphine has never tried to hurt me without my consent. She has, in fact, kept me standing on several occasions when I should not have been. "Whatever. Freedom of worship, and —"

"Yeah," said Vukradin. "Etc."

Jenna recovered. She turned to me.

She started talking about how an Uthgardt barbarian who joined the Lord's Alliance and accepted the civilizing —

I let a very loud burp out.

It echoed. It was sincere. It said everything I could have said in ten minutes of explanation, and it said it better.

She got the point.

She walked away.

I picked up my second beer. It was still good. Everything, right now, was still good.

---

## Vukradin — Planning the Next Quest

The morning we picked the Circle of Thunder, the quest list was sitting in my head like an unfinished score — three different orc problems, all of them needing to land somewhere, none of them interchangeable.

"So I want to tell you what… you want to know what Vukradin is doing in Phandalin?"

They looked at me. I spread my hands.

"So I'd like to ask, we've got three different orc… quests here."

I went through them aloud, partly for the party and partly because saying a thing clearly is how I make it make sense. "You've got the Woodland Manse." Burned, occupied, destroyed — the GM filling in what we already knew. "Falcon's Hunting Lodge got overrun." Soma started to suggest we scratch it, that we'd already fumbled that one, and I shook my head. It was still there. The problem was still there. And then: "Xanth offered to take us to the lair of the evil half-orc spellcasters." Three quests, three locations. Each one its own piece.

Soma asked if the dragon quest was still on the board. It wasn't. He's dead — Cryovain, which I will never entirely stop feeling complicated about. I added that we could still explore the Shrine of Savras, since we had never actually cleared the shrine itself, even if the orcs who had previously occupied it had already come to find us and lost that argument badly at Mountain's Toe Mine. A loose thread is a loose thread.

So: three orc problems. Which one first.

The lodge had a personal claim on me. Falcon's special wood for the studio, the venue partnership, the promise of building something real. But Falcon has not yet personally apologized to me. He attacked me at council. He stood in front of a room of people and chose the action — and yes, fine, I understand he was manipulated, or frightened, or both, and I do not blame him for the feeling. But the action was his. An apology is not a gift. It is a debt. I have not received it yet.

"I think the Falcon has not yet personally apologized to me, although he intends to, but he hasn't yet, so I'm currently inclined to go with Xanth."

Valphine was doing something with her hands. Soma nodded in that slow way she has — the one that always feels like I am being assessed by someone who has seen several of me already.

That settled it. Circle of Thunder first.

Which left the question of surviving the trip.

Soma's memory of our last time with Talosian spellcasters is more honest than mine, in the sense that she was willing to put it plainly: "We last got our asses whooped by the Talosian spellcasting orcs. It was not pleasant."

"Yeah, this might not be pleasant either, but hey."

That is the honest answer. These are half-orc spellcasters who have had their way with us before, and I have no reason to think they have gotten any easier. The difference is we are also somewhat less bad than we were. Somewhat. "Bring potions of ground," Soma said, which I took to mean potions of some sort of earthly anchoring, though she may have meant something more literal.

The lightning problem is real. I raised it because someone needed to.

"Do you need, like, lightning resistance or something like that? Because we've been lighteninged many times."

Brief technical interlude on whether it was lightning or thunder — apparently two different things, and the distinction matters. Lightning, confirmed. I pressed: "Do you want to get, like, some sort of lightning resistance? Like, we could inquire about that."

Brewbarry liked the idea. I noted, without rancor, that we don't have the money for it at the moment, but the idea was sound. Then Valphine started leafing through what she could carry into a day's work — and found something. *Protection from Energy.* Concentration, up to an hour. One target.

"Nice."

Soma flagged the cost immediately: that spell would compete with Spirit Guardians, the whirling radiant presence she summons around herself in serious fights. Right question. You don't trade one protection for another without knowing what you're giving up.

"The other concentration spells," I echoed, mostly to confirm I was tracking the logic.

Valphine kept weighing it. I left her to that. Her area, not mine.

My area was communication.

"We need to make contact with Xanth the Centaur to find out where the lair of the evil half-orc spellcasters is."

Lyra was nearby and overheard. She offered to help. I cut her off before she could finish.

"I got it."

The look on her face when she understood what I meant — *mild horror* is not too strong.

"Are you just going to be using… she suddenly has this horrified look. Are you just going to be sending messages to everybody all day?"

Soma, instantly: "I mean, that's what the spell is for!"

She is right. That is exactly what it is for. I told Lyra — and I will admit, a little delighted — "Man, I got a new spell and I really like this reaching out." Brewbarry laughed his big canyon laugh and added something about unlimited calls. I made the necessary correction: "Limited range! Any plane of existence!"

The Sending found Xanth, of course. His reply came in compressed words — the way a centaur talks when he has only so many syllables to spend. Triboar Trail, the bend toward Phandalin. We would meet him there.

"Excellent."

Resupply question before we left. Money is tight. I said it: "No money, but you guys feel free." Soma pointed out we couldn't craft anything useful from the dragon materials in Phandalin anyway. Healing potions came up. Brewbarry, in the way that is entirely Brewbarry, announced that a couple of beers had given him all the healing he required. I love this man, I genuinely do.

I ran the actual inventory. "Are we out of potions of healing? Consumables… we are out of potions. We have one potion of greater healing, and one potion of superior healing, and one scented potion of healing."

"Scented," Brewbarry confirmed, as if the word were its own complete sentence.

Valphine had a question about the superior potion — something about its contents, whether it was what it claimed to be. I caught myself mid-answer and reversed.

"Oh, oh, sorry, don't use the superior in front of me."

She looked at me. "Oh, I see." A pause. "Okay. We'll use it on you when you are unconscious."

Soma asked if she had just drunk a tainted potion. I held up a hand. "Don't tell me what happened." I meant it. "Keep me in the dark, man."

Some things I do not need to know about. Valphine is good. That is the verdict I have rendered on Valphine. The rest is Valphine's department.

We headed for the forest.

---

## Soma — Journey into the Woods

Xanthopoulos was where Vukradin's *Sending* said he would be. The bend of the Triboar Trail, the one that turns toward Phandalin. Hooves in the dirt like he'd been there a long time and had not minded it.

Centaurs do not fidget.

He was pleased. Chest first, mane second. That is how Xanth is pleased about anything.

*"My good friends, you have done such an amazing job. It was absolutely fantastic. Soma, you were superb."*

I took it the way I take most good news. Quietly. With the small private suspicion that more work was on the way.

Then Meril's name. The way it always comes up when Xanth and I talk. *Meril was very interested.* Of course he was. Meril left me a staff, a year of half-finished lessons, and whatever was left of a faith he never quite named. Xanth knows more about that than he says. I have learned not to push him on it.

The staff has been talking to me ahead of my senses for months. It has not led me wrong yet. One leaf left on it now. I try not to think about that too directly.

Boney clopped up. All bones, all dignity. The arrangement on him had been sorted earlier with less ceremony than it deserved.

*"Yeah, I mean, I'm just gonna pretend he's, you know, stomping and riding and charging and shit."*

That is my strategy. That has always been my strategy. Boney is a sensible horse in the way only skeletal horses seem to manage. He does not startle. He does not complain about the weather. He has never tried to eat my pack. Lady Alagondar made good choices, whoever she was. I respect her taste in horses.

Thirty miles. That is what a full day in the woods looks like on a map. On the legs it is something else.

The road thinned. The track thinned. The forest swallowed it gradually, the way a forest swallows anything you let it have. I read the ground the way you read anything you have been looking at long enough — lichen on the north faces, the places where animals had stopped walking, the canopy that had not been disturbed in years and the canopy that had, recently, and not by weather.

Xanth moved like a creature who belonged here. I moved behind him and almost matched it.

When the light went thin, someone asked about pressing on.

*"We're not in a rush, are we?"*

Nobody argued. Valphine had already solved camp the way she solves most things — by handing the question to whoever already had the answer. Xanth had scouted a site. Of course he had.

The fire was small. Sensible. Xanth settled beside it like a landmark settling into its proper place. Vukradin asked him for stories, which is what Vukradin does. He cannot help it.

Xanth had stories. Birds, flowers, old heroes, the complicated grievances of things older than Phandalin and older than the road we'd walked it on. He talked about Neverwinter's depredations in the tone of a creature who has watched the same mistakes pile up over centuries and developed a refined sorrow about it.

The others went polite-vacant. Eyes settling somewhere past the speaker. Faces neutral. Minds gone somewhere warmer.

I have watched shell-sprouts do this my whole life. I did not blame them. I am old. I have developed a fondness for sitting still while someone who knows more than me talks. You pick up things that way. Sometimes you pick up things you didn't know you needed.

Underneath the birds and the flowers, something colder.

He talked about the forest. The trees, the creatures, the way things had moved before Cryovain's winter broke the quiet. That much I knew. The dragon had scattered everything with sense enough to scatter.

Then he said something that sat differently.

The new orcs. The Talosian ones. Not normal orcs. Something fundamentally more evil. Something fundamentally more dangerous.

I let that sit while the fire burned down.

The forest around us felt watched in a way I could not fully account for. Not wrong, not yet. The way an old living thing watches when something has been done to it that has not finished hurting.

The others were asleep or close to it. Xanth was looking up at the canopy with the patience of a creature built to outlast things.

I listened to the trees a while longer.

Then I let myself rest.

---

## Valphine — Lore of the Storm God

The firelight was modest — just enough to push the dark back a few feet — and Xanth took up a considerable portion of that lit space, the way centaurs do, as though they had been built for amphitheatres rather than campsites. I settled into the shadow at the edge of the circle, which is where I prefer to think. The Lathanderite symbol on my chest caught what stray firelight reached me; the rest of my body did not. They have always coexisted on me without my needing to choose between them, and this fire was no different.

Vukradin opened it, the way he always opens things: with a question that sounds casual and isn't.

"Zanz, how much further to the lair of the half-orc spellcasters?"

"Another day's hike."

A beat. Then Vukradin, with that particular quality of his — the one I have catalogued as *idealism in the guise of curiosity* — leaned toward the fire and said, "Got any good stories to tell us tonight?"

The centaur's expression shifted into something that might have been fondness, or might have been the particular satisfaction of someone who had been waiting to be asked. "Stories, my friend, I have stories to tell you."

He spoke of the forest first. How it had been — not peaceful in the soft pastoral sense, but balanced, which is a different thing entirely. The white dragon had broken that balance. The animals had grown afraid. The orcs had hoarded, crowded, radicalized in the way that frightened creatures do. And these new orcs, Xanth said, were not merely dangerous in the ordinary sense. There was something *fundamentally more evil* about them, something *fundamentally more dangerous than the typical orcs*.

I filed that phrase carefully. *Fundamentally more evil.* It was theological language whether Xanth meant it that way or not. It meant something had touched their nature, not their circumstances. The word *evil* on a surface dweller's tongue is almost always a moral verdict; on Xanth's it sounded closer to a diagnosis. I appreciated the distinction.

Vukradin caught the thread. "How could they become more dangerous? What happened?"

Xanth paused — a good pause, weighted — and said: "Why, they have become members of the cult of Talos."

The name landed the way these names always land around surface dwellers: with a kind of theatrical gravity, as though saying it might summon something. I watched the campfire rather than my companions. I already knew what Talos was. I knew it the way I know most things about theological extremism — from close proximity, from having spent decades in a society that ran on divine terror, from recognizing the grammar of fanaticism in every language it has ever been spoken.

Vukradin asked where the cult originated, and Xanth drew himself up to explain.

"The story of Talos. Talos is the deity of storms and destruction. Wherever there are those who pursue destruction — wherever, and who wish to spread destruction, Talos is there. It is not… he is not… he is not in some specific place. He is in the breast of all those who seek the power to destroy, and hear his message of destruction, and revel in that destruction."

There it was. The first doctrine I ever learned in Menzoberranzan, rephrased in surface vocabulary: *the god is not a place, the god is a condition.* Lolth was the same. One could not point to where she lived and be done with her. She lived in the moments when you watched your sister's back and imagined a knife in it. She lived in ambition, in hunger, in every calculation about who could be useful and who could be discarded. The Underdark did not contain her. She contained the Underdark.

Lolth taught pain through hierarchy. Talos teaches it through incoherence. Lathander, by contrast, radiates it — openly, indifferently, on everyone — and somehow surface dwellers still mistake that for warmth. Three gods, three different relationships to the same instrument. I have spent my life inside two of them. I am beginning to understand the third.

Talos was a cruder instrument than Lolth, but the mechanics were identical: find people who already want to destroy, give them a name for the wanting, give them a doctrine that makes the wanting holy. I recognized it the way one recognizes a knife seen in a different hand.

Vukradin pressed forward, which is his nature. "What's changed recently? I mean, I'm sure Talos has been around for a long time, he's been corrupting people for centuries. Like, has something happened that he's caused him to gain lots of power recently?"

Xanth paused again. Then: "That is a very good question. Demonstrating an awareness and wisdom far beyond your age."

I will say this for Vukradin: he asks the right questions even when he does not know why they are the right questions. He has the instincts without the framework. It is like watching someone navigate a political court by feel alone — unsettling and impressive in roughly equal measure.

Xanth explained that the cult was historically small, unstable, structurally incoherent. Outlawed by every civil society worth naming. "The cult of Talos is like a disease. It explodes, it destroys everything, and then it destroys upon themselves. They are not a very — how should I say — stable god force."

He paused, and something shifted in his expression — a sidelong acknowledgment of an argument he had already rehearsed. "Adabra would say that they represent the necessary element of distraction in the cosmic balance."

I looked up at that. Interesting framing. *Distraction.* Not destruction, not evil — distraction, as though the cosmos required chaos as a corrective, a self-regulating fever. Adabra had mistaken slaughter for ecology, the way surface dwellers mistake any sustained cruelty for weather: something to be endured, named with a different word, eventually credited to the system that allowed it. I had grown up under the original of that argument. Lolth's priestesses had called it balance, too.

Xanth's voice flattened into something drier. "I would say nonsense. He's a lunatic of a god who wants to destroy things left, right, and center, and finds other stupid people who want to destroy things. And he empowers them, and they have these fantasies of destruction, and he gives them power to implement these fantasies of destruction."

*Fantasies of destruction.* There was the phrase I had been waiting for. That was the diagnostic. That was the thing that distinguished genuine theological violence from political violence dressed in religious costume — the fantasists, the ones who needed the doctrine to be true not because it gave them power but because it gave their hunger a shape it could not otherwise have. In Menzoberranzan, they were the ones who lasted longest. Not the cynical operators — those burned out or were eliminated. The true believers. The ones whose violence was an act of faith.

These orcs believed.

"So he has a new Chosen," Vukradin said.

"Yes, most likely. There is always a chosen. There's always some cleric who somehow became convinced by Talos that he has some divine message and inspiration."

"Find out," Vukradin said.

I almost smiled at that. *Find out.* As though Xanth had merely forgotten to look. But Xanth took it in stride.

"He's not in this forest, that I do know. If he was in this forest, I would know who he was, and I would be taking you there. You'd probably die, but at least we'd learn something about him." A beat. "That was a joke. I hope you appreciate the talk."

"I appreciate it," Vukradin said.

"Excellent."

The fire settled. I stayed where I was in the shadow, thinking about chosen clerics and the particular shape of conviction that turns a fanatic into a weapon. I had known priests like that. I had worked alongside them, assessed them, occasionally outmaneuvered them. They were not cautious. They were not subtle. They did not negotiate.

That, as a tactical matter, was both their greatest weakness and what made them so exceptionally dangerous.

---

## Brewbarry — The Wildcat Loggers

We were moving through the forest toward the Circle of Thunder, Xanth keeping pace alongside us, when we heard the shouting.

Not angry shouting. More like the kind of arguing that happens when people who are deeply right about something have no idea how to explain why. High-pitched, urgent, overlapping. I knew the sound before I saw who was making it.

Young druids. First season. Maybe second. The ones who still think the problem is other people not understanding what they understand.

They saw Soma's staff and it was like watching water find a crack. Suddenly all of that frantic energy had somewhere to go. They surged toward her, all of them at once, words tumbling over each other, pointing back toward the treeline where a crew of men with axes had gone very still and were watching us.

I'd seen that stillness before too. Men who work with their hands and don't trust that the people yelling at them have ever worked with theirs.

The druids' complaint came out in pieces, each one interrupting the last. Loggers. No permits. Tibor Wester — and at that name Vukradin made a sound that was less a word than a soft warning — Harbin's brother, running a wildcat operation, hiring new crews who didn't know or didn't care about the agreements that were supposed to govern this forest.

"Permits?" Soma said, and there was genuine puzzlement in her voice, the kind that makes young druids recalibrate.

The permits, it turned out, were part of an arrangement between the city of Neverwinter and the forest's caretakers. Sanctioned cutting. Agreed limits. The young druids weren't opposed to logging, they were quick to clarify — they understood the balance, they understood that dead growth had to go, that there were competing interests at stake.

"I mean, you have to," Soma said, "to protect the forest. Otherwise you get dead growth and other issues. It's just good practice."

Right. Just not this. Not men hired by a man cutting wherever the trees were thickest, with no thought for what they were taking or what would grow back.

Vukradin was trying to find the center of it. "So what's the conflict here?"

"Well, I think they want to log, and the druids don't want them to log, right?"

"Why are we against logging?"

"I mean, I think we're more against Tibor Wester than anything, aren't we?"

I was watching the loggers while this went on. Not to threaten them. Just watching. They had the look of men who'd taken work because work was available, not because they'd thought hard about who was offering it. That was a look I recognized. My people had that look, sometimes, in the years after a bad winter. You don't ask about the permits when you need to eat.

That was a thought I kept to myself.

Then Soma said something that surprised everyone, including, I think, Soma.

"We all start somewhere. You guys look like pretty naive druids as well." She was talking to the young ones, and her voice was gentle without being soft. "Why don't you show them the ropes? Show them how to properly log."

The druids blinked. The loggers blinked. There was a pause that had a different quality than the arguing.

"Can I get Vukradin's help here?"

Vukradin looked at her. "What am I saying?"

"I'm just trying to persuade them that the druids shouldn't fight them, they should use this as a teaching moment — explain to these loggers how it's correct to."

And then Vukradin opened his mouth.

I will not pretend I understood everything he said. I am a man of the stone peaks, not of the lowland forests and their civic arrangements. But I understood the shape of it. The way he talked about the forest wasn't like someone reciting rules — it had movement in it, the way good music has movement, phrases that built on each other and landed somewhere unexpected. He talked about the sanctity of what grew here, about balance, about what sustainable meant not as a regulation but as a kind of honesty between people and the land they needed. He talked about fair trade in a way that connected it to labor, to what honest work meant, to the difference between taking and receiving.

He had quips. He had something in his voice that made the whole speech feel like it was happening specifically to each person who heard it.

The axes came down.

Not dropped. Set down carefully. Which was different. Which meant something.

One of the loggers — a broad-shouldered man with the kind of face that has been weathered into something simpler than it started as — pressed the heel of his hand against his eye. He wasn't the only one. The young druids had gone quiet. The forest had gone quiet. Vukradin finished, and the loggers said they were sorry, and they said they would find honest work, and they said they would report back to the city about what Tibor Wester had been running out here.

"Wow," said Soma.

"Wow," said Vukradin. Then: "Okay, our work here is done, gentlemen."

My chest was doing something I didn't fully expect.

I've pulled trees out of the ground with my bare hands. Not many, but some. When you're large enough to do a thing and the thing needs doing, you do it. I never thought about the tree. I thought about the obstacle. I thought about what needed to move.

Standing in that forest with the loggers weeping and the druids standing quietly with their hands at their sides, I thought about the tree. I thought about all the trees.

It came out of me before I could arrange it better.

"Man, I had the tears."

Vukradin looked at me. "It's not all underhanded intimidation tactics."

"Yeah," I said. "Thinking about all the trees I've pulled out of the ground, you know."

Hands. Guilty now.

I was still thumping my chest a little, the way my body does when it doesn't know what else to do with a feeling. I'm told that contributed to the atmosphere. I believe it. The loggers were probably looking at me and thinking about a great many things they didn't want to do anymore.

But I wasn't thumping my chest to frighten them.

I was just — feeling something. The way a man does when someone puts into words the thing he didn't know he'd been carrying.

---

## Soma — The Cursed Clearing

The clearing was wrong before I stepped into it.

The staff said so first. A tremor up through the wood — the kind of feeling you get when you press a beam in an old house and the rot answers all the way through. Then the smell. Char, and something older underneath it. Nothing about a natural fire.

The pine was forty feet of black needle. Limbs burned off years ago. Nothing nested in it. Nothing sheltered under it. Even the insects gave it a wide berth, which, if you know insects, should worry you.

My one word for all of it was *"Wet."*

I meant it as a complete sentence.

Brewbarry surfaced something from his Uthgardt days. Ten little things of twigs and black hair, bundled at the base of the dead tree.

*"Black magic, voodoo, no touch. That's what Brewbarry remembers."*

Good enough. I have learned to listen when a man that large sounds that certain about something being dangerous.

Vukradin asked Xanth if this was typical Cult of Talos.

*"Mr. Vukradin. I am not a cultist of Talos. I don't know what is popular and what is not popular."* Then, after a beat: *"Good point, good point, but I know more, but not that much."*

I appreciated that. A creature who knows the edges of his own knowledge is someone I can work with.

Then the argument. I could have predicted that one before we crossed the treeline.

Brewbarry: *"Guys, I don't know much, but I do know that ghastly dolls hanging from burnt trees is probably not a good sign."*

Vukradin wanted to collect them. Then destroy them. Then burn them. Brewbarry said no touching. Vukradin pointed out we'd come here to kill the spellcasters anyway. Brewbarry, fairly, said we didn't actually know the spellcasters had made the dolls. Could be their enemies' work.

Vukradin did not appear to process this.

The staff was still uneasy, and I was still listening to it. The wrongness had saturated the soil. Roots that old grow deep and strange. Whatever ritual logic was down there had been patient.

Patient things are more dangerous than urgent ones.

I was in the middle of the clearing when Vukradin destroyed the first doll.

The pig's heart hit the ground still beating.

He destroyed the heart too.

I will not pretend I had time to think anything particularly wise in the next moment. The roots came up. I felt them before I saw them. The ground seized. Old timber, old spite, around my shins. Stuck.

The staff's tremor was not a tremor anymore. It was a shout.

I said, very calmly, in my own head: *I want to go home.*

Boney went down next to me. Faithful skeletal horse. Immune to embarrassment. Vulnerable to root traps. His bone legs went into the dirt and I thought, well. At least I have company.

Out loud I said the only useful thing: *"Anyway, when he gets knocked down, he just, you know, gets back up again."*

The roots weren't loosening. My old legs were not going to muscle through this. I made the choice without ceremony: burn a wild shape, or stay stuck in the dirt while my shell-sprouts fended for themselves.

*"Alright, we're gonna burn a wild shape into an elk."*

The giant elk. They have the weight for it. I pulled the form up from the place such forms live — the well Meril spent a year teaching me to reach into — and the clearing reorganized around the new size of me. The roots thought they had me. The roots were wrong.

Valphine's blessing was already in me, a warm current under the heave. I came free. The bark fell away. I shook it off. Then I moved to Boney, because you don't leave your people in the dirt.

Vukradin kept working. He had decided a thing needed doing and that he personally was going to do it, and nobody was to interrupt him.

Brewbarry was beside himself. *"Horrible plan. Horrible. We do no touch. That's what Brewbarry said, you're not listening."*

Valphine, with economy: *"No touching. Bad touching."*

Vukradin said he was busy and had twenty more spells to go and it would only take a couple of minutes.

I stood in the clearing in elk form, roots crumbling behind me, and watched this with the patience of a very large ruminant.

One by one the hearts fell. One by one Vukradin destroyed them. The tree stopped being what it had been. I felt it through the hooves, through the new size of me, through whatever it is the staff communicates that I still don't have good words for.

The wrongness drained. Like pressure off a wound.

When the last one was gone, the clearing went quiet in a different way. Still. The tree was just a dead tree.

Vukradin declared we had saved ten people who'd been injured by the dolls. I had doubts about the causal logic. I kept them.

*"Homer,"* he said — he always calls me Homer when he's accounting for damage — *"did you lose a total of 10 hit points?"*

*"It would have been 10, yeah."*

*"A wild shape."*

*"A wild shape."*

*"Wow,"* he said, with feeling. *"What a great trap."*

I agreed it was a great trap. I asked, just to be clear, who had sprung it.

*"That was me,"* Vukradin said.

He seemed to feel it had been worth it. He mentioned the trap-maker deserved credit for the effort.

I thought about Meril. About clearings like this, and the choices he had stood in the middle of. About what the staff had said the moment I crossed the treeline — that immediate recognition. *Not natural. Not decay. Intention.*

I had been right. The staff had been right. Knowing you're right about a bad thing doesn't keep the bad thing from happening to your legs.

Vukradin, in the voice of a man who has thought it through: *"Must fight evil!"*

I said the line that was true about me. The reason I am walking this road at forty-five with a borrowed staff and a skeletal horse and three companions I never would have predicted.

*"Must intervene."*

---

## Vukradin — The Ridge Encounter

The ridge came up fast — one moment we were picking our way across uneven ground, the next we were on the crest of it, looking across sixty feet of open air at a gully ten feet deep, and then, cresting the opposite ridge like a wave breaking, the orcs.

Ten of them. I counted. At their center, a humanoid figure with elongated claws and the particular quality of someone who has consecrated himself to a very loud god.

The battle cries hit me before I had finished counting. There is a sound that fighting people make — not the sound of people who are angry or scared or violent in the ordinary way, but the sound of people who have decided, cosmologically, that noise itself is holy. The Talosian clergy understand this. They are not trying to intimidate. They are performing.

I found this, in the moment, genuinely interesting.

Initiative. The call went up and that particular clarity settled — the moment when a situation stops being a situation and becomes, briefly, something you can navigate. I had the first opening. I knew it before the confirmation came.

"Yes, you do."

Good. Sixty feet to the opposite ridge. An acolyte who looked exactly like an acolyte — claws, posture, conviction radiating off him like heat. And around him, ten orcs who were, it occurred to me, just orcs. People with a context I did not yet fully understand. People who had probably been told a great many things about what was coming for them, very few of which would have included a bard who wanted to tell them about the wonders of Lathander.

"I'm going to use Universal Speech."

I picked targets carefully. "Targeting the leader and the three nearest him."

I thought about what I actually wanted to say. Not platitudes — Lathander, as I understand him, doesn't traffic in platitudes. Something real. Something about light as a principle rather than a weapon. The wonders. The genuine, actual wonders.

I spoke.

The cleric did not receive it well. I was told — as a courtesy, and I appreciated the honesty — that it was not going to work on him. That it had, in fact, enraged him a little bit more.

"Okay," I said. "Well. Maybe the other three."

And the other three: something shifted. Not conversion. Not surrender. The slowing that happens when an idea enters a mind that wasn't expecting one. They would still come forward, of course they would — momentum, companions, screaming cleric behind them — but they would not rush. They would move at the pace of people who had heard something unexpected.

I considered that a successful opening verse.

"And once I've cast a spell, I can use that again. Which I will plan on doing for the others as we go."

A gentle caution from somewhere to my left: proselytizing about Lathander would be less effective once the combat actually started, if I understood the warning correctly.

"I mean, if we attack," I said. I thought it was obvious, but I said it anyway. "I'm here to proselytize about Lathander. For now."

There is a position I have held for years, and I hold it still: most conflicts are misunderstandings conducted at escalating volume, and the solution is almost never to match the volume. The solution is the frequency underneath the noise that people actually respond to. Not everyone. Not all at once. Three orcs who might slow down. Then three more. Then the situation has changed.

Valphine, moving next, was working through her options. The lightning resistance came up briefly and passed. Then she said, in the particular tone she uses when an idea is both practical and doctrinally significant:

"Well, I can cast Daylight."

I squinted. The sun was already out. As I pointed out, quite sunny.

"It's sunny out."

Brewbarry, to his credit, saw something in it. "Yeah, man, they're not wearing sunglasses. Maybe they could be blinded by the daylight."

I considered it. There is something theologically elegant about the idea of Lathander's light being so intense it overwhelms the uninitiated. Something that works as metaphor and as tactics simultaneously.

"Blinded by Lathander's glory," I said.

Valphine settled on her holy symbol as the vessel, and the light came.

I was standing behind her when it happened, which I suspect is where one wants to be. Sixty feet in every direction, blazing and absolute, the kind of brightness that doesn't ask permission. The opposite ridge was flooded. The orcs were flooded. And the Talosian cleric, caught in the full wash of a light his entire theology identifies as an affront —

He screamed.

"Kill the false cleric of Lathander! Kill the drow cleric of Lathander, the abomination! Destroy! Destroy the false god!"

Soma, who has more patience for this kind of categorical error than I do, objected on Valphine's behalf: "She's not false, she's the real deal."

Exactly correct. I doubted the cleric was in a position to receive the clarification.

I looked across the gully. The light. The orcs, some slowing, some still screaming, and the cleric in the center of it all committing entirely to the wrong reading of what was happening. He thought we were here to fight him. He thought the light was a weapon. He thought Valphine was an abomination, which — and I say this with genuine respect for Valphine — he had badly miscalculated in the direction of his own destruction.

We were not here to fight. We were here to resolve a misunderstanding.

The cleric, however, was not a misunderstanding. He was the reason the misunderstanding had been allowed to grow into an army.

He's evil. That is the verdict. The orcs are not. Two different problems.

"We'll have to focus all of our attacks only on the leader," I said, and I meant it, "and try to convert the rest."

A pause from someone nearby. Some flicker of disbelief at how this fight was apparently going to be conducted.

"Alright," I said. "Sounds good."
# Chapter 41 Through the valley to the top of the hill


---

## Soma — Recap And Battle Setup

The gully was about sixty feet across. I clocked that first — width, depth, the angle of the far ridge. Ten orcs on the opposite side, and one anchorite of Talos with claws where fingers should be. The light was wrong on her. Not blight-wrong, not the wrongness I'd learned to read through the staff, but wrong in the way that something has been dedicated to cruelty for long enough that the cruelty shows in the posture.

I thought of Corbin, briefly. Couldn't help it. He'd be at Boney's flank right now, nervous, trying to prove something. But Corbin was dead, and we were here partly because of that, and I wasn't going to let the thought sit any longer than it took to name it.

Vukradin was already talking. He had launched into something about Lathander — I caught the shape of it, the cadence he uses when he's trying to reach people who weren't planning on being reached. Three of the orcs nearest the anchorite shifted. Not friendly. Not close to friendly. But the particular posture that means *I am listening instead of swinging,* which is more than I'd expected from orcs under a Talosian caster's authority.

Then Valphine let the radiant light bloom from her hands.

The anchorite's reaction was immediate. You didn't need to speak Orcish or Common or any language at all to read what happened next — she named Valphine a false cleric and the order went down the line of orcs like a stone through water. The three that Vukradin had reached with his words were still hesitating, but the rest had made their decision.

Vukradin said something about having cast the whole speech in Orcish. There was a long beat.

"I made a point of talking in orc," he said, and the tone was a man discovering he'd paid for a very specific service that the room didn't require.

Valphine told him she spoke Orcish too. He received this information with the particular stillness of someone calculating exactly how many of his special abilities he had just spent unnecessarily.

Orcs on the ridge. Anchorite with claws. Three neutrals who might hold if nobody did anything else too dramatic.

The battle for the Circle of Thunder was about to begin.

---

## Brewbarry — The Battle For The Circle Of Thunder

The orc came out of nowhere, screaming for Talos.

I heard it before I saw it — that rising battle-cry, the kind that's meant to rattle you, and I felt Vukradin shift beside me. The big one, the one they'd call Orc 2 if this were a ledger entry and not a gully full of killing, had his greataxe up and was charging straight at Vukradin with everything he had.

And then something strange happened.

Vukradin did that thing he does — that thing I still don't fully understand, where the air around him gets a little heavier, a little more intentional, and the world sort of bends to accommodate his will. The orc swung. The blow that should have connected just... didn't. It went wide. I felt the advantage of it pass into me like heat from a fire, a certainty in my hands I don't usually have until I'm already bleeding. Vukradin's voice, calm behind me: *We'll give Brewbarry advantage on his next attack.*

That's Vukradin. That's always been Vukradin. He takes a hit that was meant to hurt him and turns it into something useful for me.

I didn't have long to feel grateful.

The anchorite hit us all at once.

Lightning doesn't feel like much in the instant it touches you — it's the half-second after, when every muscle in your body seizes and your teeth crack together and the light burns a white line across your vision. The bolt came down the gully and found Vukradin, found Xanth, found me. I heard the centaur curse in words I didn't know, the kind of raw syllables that mean the same thing in every language. I was still standing — barely — but the hit had reorganized something inside me, pulled the air out of my chest and replaced it with a kind of ringing absence. The anchorite stood at the far end of the field looking pleased with himself.

That was a mistake on his part.

Xanth got his longbow up fast — two shots, both of them high, lost in the trees. He looked disgusted with himself in the way only someone who genuinely expected better can look.

Then Soma moved.

I have watched Soma transform before. It never gets less strange. One moment there is a tortle elder, patient and heavy-shelled, and then the air warps and there is something enormous where she was — a giant elk, head down, already moving, already building speed before the form has fully settled. She hit the anchorite like a wall of forest. The ram drove him into the dirt and kept going, and when the dust cleared he was on his belly, prone, and Soma's voice came out of that massive throat with something like satisfaction: *On your belly.*

The anchorite had a moment to consider what it meant to insult a druid.

Around me, the orcs were finding their angles. One went for Vukradin again. Another tried Soma's elk form and missed. A third — one of the ones that was supposed to be neutral, which is a thing I find funny, the idea of a neutral orc in a fight — launched a javelin at the elk and got through. I saw Soma absorb it. She didn't go down, but she was eating damage now, which meant the clock was running.

Then Boney arrived.

Boney is a skeleton on a horse. I mean — Boney is a skeletal horse who carries a sword and fights like he knows what he's doing, because apparently that is a thing that happens when Soma is involved. He came through the middle of everything, found the prone anchorite, and hit him hard with that longsword. Two-handed, because Boney doesn't carry a shield. Of course he doesn't. He's a skeleton. I found myself briefly grateful that I didn't have to explain this to myself anymore.

The anchorite was still breathing. Not for long.

Orc 7 decided to charge into the cluster of us, which was brave, if unwise. My body moved before I decided to move — the halberd was already coming up, the first swing gone wide, and then Vukradin's gift was still in my hands, the advantage still warm, and the second swing connected with everything I had behind it. The orc went down hard and didn't get up.

From somewhere to my left, Vukradin's voice carried that particular note of someone who is trying to sound irritated but is actually just amused:

*"How are we gonna win them over if you're slaughtering them?"*

I didn't have an answer for that. The orc had charged. The sword was already out. What exactly was I supposed to do.

Valphine spoke for me, which was fair: *"But he came to attack us."*

And then it was my turn.

I raged. There is something that happens in that moment — not loss of self, not quite, but a simplification. The gully got cleaner. The anchorite was prone. He had lit up Vukradin with lightning. He had lit up Vukradin.

I moved through the two orcs between me and the anchorite. They both took their swings. Neither of them connected. Sometimes the world wants you to get somewhere, and it steps aside. I brought the halberd down on the prone anchorite — once, with the weight of Bless behind it, with the certainty of Vukradin's gift still singing faintly in my muscles — and the hit was clean and total. I could feel how little was left in him.

The second swing missed. But then Soma pointed out the obvious thing — he was prone, which meant I had advantage — and Valphine rolled again.

Eighteen.

The anchorite died.

Vukradin: *"Alright!"* And then, because he is who he is: *"No more killing things, let's convert everybody!"*

I stood over the body and thought about that for a moment.

Orc 9 came at Boney next, which I hadn't expected — something about the skeleton offended him, maybe, or maybe Boney just had the look of something valuable. I saw the swing coming and I stepped into it. The hit landed on me instead. While raging it felt like being tapped on a bruise — real, but containable. Boney lived. I figured Soma would want that.

On the other side of the gully, Orc 10 threw a javelin at Valphine and missed completely, the kind of miss that has a story behind it. Orc 11 got through the elk's side for something.

Then Orc 2 — the first one, the one Vukradin had redirected — apparently decided he'd been patient enough with all this fighting. He put his greataxe down. Not dropped it. Set it down. Deliberate. And then he said, in the way that men say things when they've run the numbers and don't like the result:

*"Give me money and I let you live."*

I looked at Vukradin. Vukradin looked at the orc.

*"The followers of Lathander don't make such demands."*

The orc picked his greataxe back up. Of course he did. He swung. And I heard, underneath the impact, underneath Vukradin's grunt of pain, the orc's whole logic laid out in the way he pulled back: *I don't want to kill you, man, I just want the money.*

Xanth's second round of shots went high. Both of them.

And then Soma, who had been taking hits in elk form and absorbing them one by one, made a decision. She stepped back, took the attacks of opportunity that came with moving — one of them connecting, one glancing off nothing — and then she dropped the form. Just let it go. The elk vanished. Soma was a tortle again, smaller, standing in the middle of a gully full of orcs, and she climbed onto Boney's back like it was the most natural thing in the world.

*"So we get the abomination and the delicious meat away from the guys,"* she said.

Boney moved. Orc 9 swung at him as he went. Missed.

And that was how it sat — the anchorite dead in the dirt, the orcs still circling, the gully still loud with the smell of lightning and blood and something that might have been possibility, if Vukradin had anything to say about it.

He usually did.

---

## Valphine — The Rout Of The Talosians

The anchorite went down hard. Brewbarry's axe found him before the man had finished a prayer, and I watched the last breath leave a fanatic of Talos with the same clinical attention I bring to most deaths — cataloguing it. The grammar of that moment: a priest of the storm-god, prone, exposed, cut down by a Goliath who was running through javelin fire to get there. Clean. I had assessed the tactical situation and directed Brewbarry toward the more dangerous caster first. In Menzoberranzan, you kill the spellcaster. You kill the spellcaster before anything else. Some lessons survive the border crossing.

I am not without sympathy for what Talos offers. I understand the appeal of a violent god — the permission structure, the theology that places destruction at the center rather than at the margin. In House Sotorra, cruelty was doctrine. Not worship exactly, but something adjacent: the acknowledgment that power expresses itself through pain, and that the god who sanctions your pain is the god worth serving. I have known that grammar. I left it behind not because it was cruel but because it was *small* — rationed through hierarchy, spent carefully, always in danger of running out. Talos is the same operation. Storms end. The sun does not.

Still. The priest had believed in something. That is worth noting.

Vukradin was already speaking in rounds, his voice working the gully below with something that is, I think, the most honest magic he does. Universal Speech is a strange faculty — not persuasion exactly, more like the removal of a barrier, the linguistic distance collapsed so that the argument can reach the person directly. He rolled a twenty-six. I watched the orcs on the ridgeline go through several stages in rapid succession: hostility, calculation, the particular slowing that happens when an idea enters a mind that wasn't expecting one. By the time he finished the passage, he had moved seven of them away from the fight. He had been speaking to Lathander the entire time before he corrected himself to say it. The slip was interesting. I filed it away.

My own contribution was less elegant.

The orcs speak their own language and I speak it too — one of many things from my education I have never bothered to discard. I called on them to kneel before the power of Lathander. I said it with the register one uses for commands to inferiors, which in my experience functions as a reasonable default. What I had not sufficiently accounted for was the compound liability: drow, undead skeletal horse, unstructured presentation, mid-combat exhortation. The orcs did not find the combination inspiring. One who had been neutral reconsidered his neutrality in my direction and returned to hostility. I was informed, with some diplomatic candor, that *orcs don't like drows.* This is not untrue. And I was informed that *this was not the best organized religious ceremony.* This is also not untrue.

The truth is that a drow cleric of Lathander leading a disorganized warband that includes a skeletal horse and a barbarian in a dread helm with glowing red eyes does not read as a coherent theological proposition to an orc who was already uncertain. Surface religious ceremonies have *structure* for a reason — ritual is the scaffolding that makes unfamiliar power legible. We had offered none. We had offered combat and a persuasive aasimar bard, which is better than nothing but not quite a creed.

*We gotta work on the spectacle a bit,* Vukradin said, which was rueful enough that I nearly said something kind in response. I didn't.

Brewbarry sent one fleeing orc off with a swing that missed — on purpose, we agreed, in the way that certain misses are on purpose, or at least that is how I have elected to record it. The halberd said *who has the violence*. The miss said *you are not worth the expenditure*. The orc understood both messages and ran. That is a reasonable outcome.

Orc nine did not receive the same consideration. I told Brewbarry to stomp him, and Brewbarry did, with the kind of directness that makes him an effective ally and a suboptimal negotiating partner. The non-lethal call arrived a moment too late. Someone noted it. Then: *too late.* Then: *alright, next time.* Vukradin was rueful again. I said, dryly, that Brewbarry would say *oops, sorry*, which is approximately what happened. The orc was dead. We had not intended it. These things accumulate.

Orc ten was handled more precisely. I called the target, declared the strike non-lethal with enough lead time to matter, and Brewbarry put the orc down cleanly, unconscious. Fifteen points of force through a non-lethal strike. One hit. The orc crumpled and stayed. Good. I had wanted at least one of them awake for afterward.

Then the flight.

There is a specific quality to the moment when a warband decides to stop being one. It does not happen in unison — it cannot, because each individual is performing a private calculation, and those calculations do not complete simultaneously. What you observe from the outside is a cascade: one orc decides the arithmetic no longer works, turns, runs. The next sees him go and revises his own figures. Then another. The whole structure dissolves not because anyone surrendered but because everyone, separately, concluded that the available options had narrowed to survival.

Orcs one, four, five, and eight. Then eleven. Then six — who *had* been receptive, who had been moving toward the argument, who looked around at the field and the fleeing companions and the bright light that is deliciously painful for me and decided that life was too short. He ran. I watched him go.

Vukradin called out to orc three as the man bolted: *see the way to Lathander!* The invitation was genuine, which is one of the more interesting things about him. He converts by reflex. He cannot watch a man run away from an argument without wanting to give him the last line. Orc three ran anyway.

What I felt, watching the gully empty, was not triumph. Something more complicated than that — the specific satisfaction of seeing a violent hierarchy disassemble, knowing I understand every structural reason it held together as long as it did and every structural reason it could not hold any longer. The anchorite was the keystone. Brewbarry removed him in the first exchange. Without the spellcaster, without the holy sanction, the orcs were a warband without architecture. Even the one who had believed — even the one who had thrown his javelin at the skeletal horse because an undead abomination offended his god — eventually ran.

I have known worse hierarchies than this one. I have served inside them, been assessed by them, been found insufficient by them. There is a particular flavour of satisfaction in watching the machinery of a smaller power come apart, when you are standing in the light of a larger one.

The gully was quiet. One orc unconscious. The rest: fled or dead.

Vukradin had been speaking to Lathander before he corrected himself.

I did not say anything about that.

---

## Vukradin — The Conversion Of Prutha

The last orc standing looked at me with the specific expression of a man who has just watched nine of his fellows die and is working out the arithmetic of the situation. He was holding his greataxe. I was watching his eyes.

I said everything I had to say to him. The words came from the same place they always come from — not performance, not calculation, but the genuine conviction that there is a true frame available to any moment and I am reaching for it. The sun above the gully. The Drow cleric wreathed in impossible light. The dead anchorite of Talos cooling behind us. I laid it out for him. The picture was honest. It required no embellishment.

He set down the greataxe.

He looked at Valphine — this radiant, painful, sunlit figure that no orc who grew up praying to the Stormlord could have anticipated encountering in a forest gully — and the working-out in his eyes resolved. He spoke in halting Common, his voice somewhere between wonder and practical assessment.

"Talos offer power. Lathander — more power. Lathander all-powerful."

Then he rushed toward Valphine and announced himself a follower of the Drow Cleric of Lathander.

I said, honestly: *"Wow. We've got a follower!"*

Because that was exactly what we had.

His name was Prutha. The party began debating conversion names before I could object — which I did, loudly, the moment Valphine suggested *Thrall.*

"Harsh, man, harsh. Wow." I let the word sit there. Then: "You know, I object. You know, he doesn't know what thrall means, but I know what thrall means. That is not appropriate for our new friend."

Prutha kept his name. As it should be.

What he told us next required more than just the one moment to take in. His great-uncle had been his clan's shaman. The Talosians killed him deliberately, early, to break the clan's resistance and make recruitment easier. They called the old man weak, abomination, thunder meat. And then they stood in front of what remained of his family and offered the terms Talos always offers: fight, or be what his great-uncle was.

Prutha had fought. Three skirmishes. Never killed by choice.

I thought about Corbin — briefly, painfully, the way I always think about Corbin now, a flash of the face and then the weight settling. I had pushed a man into something similar and called it recruiting. I wasn't going to do that accounting here, in the middle of a gully. But the thought was present.

Then Prutha reached into his clothing and produced a small bone whistle.

He explained that in his clan, the orcs had greeted the sunrise each morning by blowing a bone whistle. Eastern tradition, his great-uncle's tradition. He held it up. He looked at it for a long moment.

And then he blew it.

One note. Simple and thin and very old.

And then he began to cry.

Valphine read him with a sharpness I could not have matched — later she told me her read was simply that he'd realized how long it had been since he last blew it. That was what the tears were for. Not the dead uncle. Not the three skirmishes. Not the men who died in the gully behind him. The whistle. The gap between the whistle then and the whistle now.

I found I had nothing to say for a moment.

Then Prutha gave us the line his great-uncle had apparently lived by, the thing the old shaman had passed down before the Talosians named him thunder meat and put him in the ground:

*"Dawn comes for everyone, even those born in shadow."*

The table went quiet.

"Wow," I said. "It's quite poetic."

I meant it completely. I said to Prutha — honestly, reaching for the right thing to say to a man who had just blown a whistle for the first time in what seemed like years: "You're my first."

And then the thought arrived, the one I voiced aloud because it was obvious and true: "He wants to play the whistle at the dawn, but with Lathander, it's like it's the dawn all the time. So, like, he could play the whistle all the time."

The theology here was not complicated. Lathander is perpetual dawn. The whistle greets the dawn. The math resolves. I was genuinely pleased with how cleanly it fit.

Valphine reached for a Religion assessment of the situation and came back with a result she described only as "oh my god" in a tone that suggested the dice had not cooperated. Despite this, some kind of genuine insight arrived anyway — the notion that the whistle ritual could be woven into her own evolving practice, that Lathander was not moving further from her for it, but closer. I thought about Valphine's church, which the party had described diplomatically as a masochism cult, and then thought about the bone whistle and the weeping orc and the words about dawn and shadow, and I thought: well, this is how religions acquire depth. It is not always tidy.

I turned to Prutha and delivered what I had to give him.

"Lathander blesses you today, my child."

He looked at me. "What does that mean?"

"Lathander blesses you today, my child."

He thought about it. Then: "He thinks that's awesome." He had, apparently, lots to think about.

"Lathander — power. Beyond doubt. Lathander all-powerful." He turned back to Valphine and pledged himself again, firmly, in case anyone had missed it the first time.

Then he kicked the fallen anchorite's body several times to make a point about theological transition.

I disapproved of the corpse-stringing that followed — when Valphine and Brewbarry hauled the anchorite up as a warning, Prutha was visibly enthusiastic in a way that landed somewhere I preferred not to examine — but I didn't intervene. I had a follower. He had just blown a bone whistle and wept and recited a line of genuine beauty in his second language. I was prepared to allow him the kicks.

He laid out his terms for the path forward: orcs no longer following Talos, we spare. Committed Talosians are another matter entirely.

Convert or die. A fluid approach to religion, yes. But it worked for the anchorite in the other direction, didn't it? The Talosians had offered exactly that framing to Prutha's great-uncle, and the only difference between that moment and this one is which door leads somewhere worth walking through.

I asked about the orc who was still unconscious somewhere behind us. Whether he might be revivable, convertible, another Prutha waiting to emerge.

The answer was uncertain. We pressed on.

Someone — I will not say who — made a joke about whether Corbin would have liked Prutha.

The DM's response was that it was cold.

He was right. It was cold. And also, yes. Corbin would have liked Prutha very much. He would have recognized something in the whistle, in the terms offered and refused and survived through compromise, in the great-uncle's line about dawn and shadow. He would have been moved by it.

I was moved by it. I was carrying that, along with everything else.

---

## Soma — Arrival At The Circle Of Thunder

The last thing Xanth did before he left was make everyone uncomfortable.

He stood there, that enormous centaur, and looked at the staff the way you look at something you already know the history of. Not like he was admiring it. Like he was remembering. Then he turned to me — tapped me, actually, on the shell, his hand broad enough to cover half of it — and said, "This one, this one was blessed by Meril, and I know that she will do great things. Peace, Beauty."

Shell-sprouts. The whole lot of them were watching me after that.

I did not say anything. There is not much to say when a centaur you met two days ago understands something about you that you are still arguing with yourself about in the dark hours before dawn. The staff sat in my grip, quiet. Three leafs on the thing. I have been watching those leaves since Xanth told me Meril chose me on purpose, which is the kind of information you receive and then carry at arm's length while you figure out what to do with it.

Xanth looked at the staff one final time. Just looked at it. He was doing something with that look — measuring, or saying goodbye to it, or confirming something for himself — and yes, it made everybody feel a bit awkward. Vukradin broke the silence first, because Vukradin always breaks the silence first.

"Hooves off," he said, appreciating the phrase as Xanth did exactly that.

I watched the centaur go until the trees took him. Then: "You call that hooving. I'll show you hooving."

Nobody asked what I meant by that. Good. I wasn't sure I knew.

Prutha filled the space that Xanth left. She has that gift — or it is something else — of knowing exactly how to push forward when standing still feels like a waste of everyone's time. "We go kill other Talosian clerics," she said, and that was the plan summarized. Vukradin fussed with the name of the quest for a moment, the way he does when he needs to feel like things are organized properly: *Xanth the Centaur has offered to take us to the lair of the evil half-orc spellcasters.* Yes. And now Xanth had done his part. So.

We walked.

The hill rose out of the treeline before the storm did, which meant I saw it first as a shape — ninety feet of slope, trees gripping the sides of it like they were holding on. And then the clouds. They were already there above the crest, the kind of grey-green build that means something is gathering itself on purpose. Not weather. Intent.

The prepared description came all at once when we cleared the trees: a ring of standing stones at the summit, ancient and deliberate, and inside the ring — two figures moving. Dancing, in the loose sense of the word, in that way that is less celebration and more negotiation with something that does not speak. And around them: small, twitching, many-limbed shapes, capering.

"They're doing, like, a fire dance around it?" I asked.

"I guess you could say that."

Twig blights. Twelve of them, once we counted. I know twig blights. Every druid knows twig blights — they are the forest's bad faith argument, the thing that wears roots like a costume. Intelligence of four, which means instinct and malice and nothing else. Not convertible, I was told, as if I had been about to suggest a conversion.

The staff moved. Not visibly. It is never visible. But there is a difference between holding a piece of old wood and holding something that is paying attention, and standing at the edge of that clearing, looking up at the henge and the storm and the dancing figures, I felt very clearly that the staff was paying attention.

Meril, I thought, and did not finish the thought.

Whatever he had brought here — whatever he had walked toward in his last years, whatever had drawn him to this region and this particular rot in the world — it was up that hill. The Circle of Thunder had been there the whole time, waiting. And here I was at the treeline with one leaf left on a borrowed staff, arguing with Vukradin about a necklace.

"We do!" I said, because we were already into it. "I keep telling you we do."

"And I keep telling you, we don't, we're not allowed to use that, it's not ours. I am holding on to this necklace, you are not — I don't trust you with it."

I did not have time for this. I also did not want to say that what I was actually thinking about was not the necklace at all but the way the staff had just shifted in my hand, subtle as a change in tide direction, some dormant quality of it waking up in response to whatever was saturating the air at the top of that hill.

"Hey, look over there!" Tactically useful, also accurate. "Okay, they're not even — they're not clustered enough for Fireball. They're not even clustered for it."

Vukradin had something cone-shaped. He mentioned it. Valphine offered Spirit Guardians, which was sensible. "Spirit Guardians plus Dash," Vukradin said, and something about that combination appealed to him in a planning way that I recognized. "Anyway, I've got, like, Thunderwave or something, I think that works pretty well, right? Like — Thunderwave, oh..."

The hill was still there. The storm was still building. The figures in the henge were still moving.

I held the staff and looked up at the standing stones and thought three leaves. At least there wasn't a fourth. 

We stayed at the treeline and studied what we were walking into.

# Chapter 42 — Unraveling the Storm God's Secrets

## Vukradin — Pre Battle Observations At The Circle Of Thunder

The hill had been climbing for most of the afternoon, and then it stopped. The treeline thinned and there it was — a ring of standing stones against a sky that hadn't decided whether to storm. The clouds above the henge moved the way clouds don't move: inward, circling, held in place by something that wasn't wind.

Two half-orcs stood among the stones. Twelve twig blights ranged around them like a second ring, bark-dry and motionless. The half-orcs were moving — not marching, not chanting. Dancing. Slow, deliberate steps that traced a pattern I couldn't fully see from the treeline but could feel the shape of: something being called toward. Something being opened.

Corbin, I thought. Then I pushed the thought somewhere useful.

Valphine was the one who named it. She watched for a moment, head tilted, that particular stillness she gets when she's cataloguing rather than reacting. "Summoning ritual," she said. Quiet, certain. The way she identifies things she's seen before.

I looked at the dancers again with that frame on them. "Oh, yeah, you would recognize that in this," I said. "Animate Dead." Not a question. The motion had that quality — purposeful vacancy, movement in service of something absent.

Soma watched. Brewbarry watched. Neither of them saw it the way Valphine did, and I was moving through the same fog — you don't spend your early years in Phandalin studying Talosian summoning rites. What I felt was the thing underneath the recognition: we were already late. Whatever they were calling, they had been at it for a while.

"I wonder who they're summoning," I said.

"I mean, you'll find out," came back at me from somewhere to my left, dry as bark.

"No, we won't."

There are promises you make in a treeline. I meant it as one.

The tactical question resolved itself quickly in my mind into a single clean answer: Silence. You cast it on the chanters, you cut the ritual at its voice. I had used it before, at the lighthouse, at worse angles. "Alright, I'm gonna cast Silence," I said. "And I, once again, have no, like, connection to the board, so — but I am casting silence on whoever it is is chanting." I kept my voice level. "And if that is unknown, then the two spellcasters."

Except they weren't chanting. That was the thing. We waited, someone went back through the logic of it, and the answer came back clear and slightly absurd: the ritual had no vocal component. They were dancing. Twelve twig blights and two half-orcs turning slow deliberate circles in a stone ring, silent as a held breath.

"Is there no vocal component to the ritual?" I asked, already hearing the answer.

There wasn't.

"Awesome," I said. The word landed flatter than I intended.

I filed the Silence away. "I mean, if there's no vocal component, there's whole person — that's also an option." Hold Person. Different spell, same interruption. The ritual, we determined, would end only when the dancers stopped. The standing stones couldn't be disrupted from the outside; the movement had to cease. Which meant the people making it had to cease.

Brewbarry was watching the half-orcs step their slow circles in total silence. "So they're like, what, a pantomime club?" he said.

I looked at him. I looked at the henge. "Okay, guys," I said. "Do you want me to go with Silence or Hold Person?"

Before anyone answered, someone caught the gap: we hadn't rolled initiatives yet. The observation arrived with that particular mild embarrassment of a procedural thing almost skipped over in the press of the moment.

We rolled. I drew the short straw on the tie-breakers — except I didn't. I won them. Several, one after another, my name settling ahead of the others in the order like the situation had opinions. I had no strong feelings about going first. I had feelings about what going first meant I would have to do.

"Alright," I said, once the order was settled and clear. "So I've not cast Silence — because we're following initiative order, alright?"

The hill was still there. The stones were still there. The dancers had not stopped.

---

## Brewbarry — The Battle At The Circle Of Thunder

Twelve of them.

Vukradin said "Two twigs and an anchorite — the start of a joke," and he wasn't wrong, but twelve is not a joke. Twelve is a wall of dry, clacking wood and too many limbs, and they came fast. I was already moving.

That's the thing about the rage. People think it makes you stupid. It doesn't. It narrows everything down to what matters — where the threat is, where the gap is, where you can put your body to do the most good. The hill was steep and the standing stones were wrong, humming at a frequency that made my back teeth ache, and the two half-orcs at the center of it all were still dancing, still chanting, and I wanted to be the thing that made them stop.

The lightning bolt came before I reached them.

Vukradin had already said it, dry as old bark: "It's nice that we're all lined up in a perfect line there — that's convenient for him." He wasn't wrong about that either. The bolt split the air between us and I got my shoulder turned into it and the current raked through my scale mail and I was still standing because I am Brewbarry Root Smasher Ogalakadu and I have stood inside a dragon's breath, and a half-orc in a boar mask is not a dragon. Valphine took it worse. I saw her flinch — something going tight across her face that she would never call pain but that looked exactly like it. The invisible weight of Lathander's favor pressing on every swing, and it still turned against her twice. Some days the gods are funny.

Vukradin didn't waste the opening. He spoke and the two anchorites stopped dancing. Just — stopped. Mid-step, mid-chant, arms out, frozen like figures in a story someone stopped telling. She stopped them. Both of them. I've seen him do things with words that make no sense to me and probably never will, but this I understood immediately: they were objects now. Problems with a shape. I moved.

The handaxe is not my preferred statement. I am a big man with a big sword and I know how to use it, but the blights were between me and the anchorites and the blights needed clearing, so I pulled the rage up from wherever it lives in my chest — it feels like a door opening, every time, like something I've been keeping in a small room finally being let out — and I threw.

The first throw was embarrassing. The axe spun wide and I had a half-second of pure goliath shame before Valphine pushed something of her certainty into my hand, metaphorically speaking. Something steadied. The axe was already back in my hand — it comes back, that's the trick, that's what I've been calling the Elemental Cleaver, because naming things makes them more real — and I adjusted and threw again and the blight I hit came apart like kindling. The momentum carried: one blight dead, the kill gave me a heartbeat of something clear and sharp, and I used it to take a second. Two down. One more and I missed, and by then the battlefield was moving around me in all directions.

Boney bit a paralyzed anchorite. The skeletal horse that Soma has somehow convinced is a willing member of this party bit a frozen man in a boar mask and I respect that completely.

Prutha ran through blights like they were grass. He put a javelin into the second anchorite and then charged in with his greataxe and I watched him and thought, briefly, of myself ten years younger, when violence was still simple, before the exile made it complicated. The anchorite he hit was already staggered. Not down, but close.

Soma became an elk. I have seen this before and it still takes a moment. One second: Soma, tortle, shell, old and unhurried. Next second: enormous antlers, enormous mass, crossing the ground between them in a breath. She hit the anchorite like a wall of forest deciding to move. He didn't have a choice about it.

Then she turned and hit one of the standing stones.

I thought: is that part of it? The henge was wrong, humming, tainted — Talosian hands had been on it, doing whatever ritual left a deer split open at the center with its heart replaced by something black and glassy and cold. Breaking a stone felt right. Felt like undoing something.

Valphine was moving through the twig blights like a woman who finds this situation aesthetically appropriate. The radiant presences she called up swirled around her and the blights caught in them just — went. She crossed the field and the light went with her, sweeping the dry things from the hill in waves, and I kept count because counting kept me sharp.

The anchorites never got free. Vukradin said, somewhere to my left, "Stopping a man in his tracks — both men — that is a very powerful thing," the way a man says something he already knew but is pleased to have confirmed.

At the end, Valphine said her battle cry. She said: *"Die ye then."*

She hit the last anchorite and he went down and the chant that had been threading through the air for however long we'd been on this hill — it stopped. The clouds kept moving for a moment, like they hadn't been told yet. Then they peeled back. Slow. Reluctant. Like something exhaling. The pressure in my ears dropped. The ozone smell faded to wet leaves and old rain. The stones went quiet.

No thunderclap. Just the end of it.

I stood in the sudden silence and looked at the two bodies. Young, both of them. Younger than I expected under the boar masks. One with storm-cloud tattoos spiraling up his neck, each one with an open eye. The other with crossed boar tusks down both forearms. They'd been someone's devoted. Someone had put that ink in their skin and told them this mattered, and they'd believed it, and now they were dead on a hill in the Neverwinter Wood with their masks rolled free of their faces.

I didn't feel bad about it. I felt the way I always feel after a fight: present, tired in the right way, aware of every part of my body. Alive.

Vukradin called it: "Huzzah!"

I exhaled.

---

## Soma — Aftermath And Ideological Clashes

The ozone went first. Then the pressure in my ears released — not all at once, but in slow degrees, like something enormous exhaling. The clouds peeled back from the henge in a reluctant spiral, and the standing stones, which had been humming through my boot soles since we crested the hill, went inert without ceremony. No thunderclap. Just wet leaves and old rain, and the ordinary smell of a forest after weather.

I stood still for a moment and let the quiet settle.

It's a druidic site. That was the thing I kept returning to as I walked the circle. Valphine had asked it and gotten confirmation — anchorites don't build henges, they borrow them. Someone had stood here before Talos claimed it. Someone had read the standing stones as sacred in a different register entirely, and whatever ritual they had meant to conduct here had been slowly replaced, glyph by glyph, with something that killed deer and summoned storm and hummed with a frequency that made my back teeth ache.

The deer was at the center. I didn't approach it at first. I noted it from the edge of the circle the way you note a thing you will have to reckon with in a moment.

When I did walk over, the smell hit me: blood, cooled, and something underneath that had no name yet. The animal had been split throat to belly, a clean and deliberate cut, and where the heart should have been there was a hollow of black, glassy material. Not stone. Not metal. Cool to the touch, faintly humming the way the stones had been humming a minute ago. I put two fingers near it and pulled them back.

I have seen a blighted grove. I have seen what happens when something reaches into a living system and begins redirecting it. This was that, except it had been done to a specific animal, at a specific moment, for a specific purpose. The deer had been chosen. The thought sat in me like a stone.

The anchorites were younger than I expected. I looked at their faces after the boar masks rolled free — young half-orcs, the kind of young where the face still carries some softness under the tattoos. One had storm clouds and coiling spirals up his neck, each spiral containing an open eye. The other had crossed boar tusks repeated down both forearms in a different hand but the same ink. They had been marked by someone who knew what they were doing. Someone who had wanted them to carry Talos on their skin.

I did not grieve them. I want to be honest about that. But I noted the youth, and I noted the tattoos, and I thought about what Adabra had called me at the council — interventionist, as if that were a diagnosis — and I thought about what it had taken to get here, and whether the intervention had been clean.

It hadn't been clean. It rarely is.

The argument started almost before the blood had dried.

Vukradin moved toward the bodies with the particular energy he gets when a principle is at stake. Holy symbols of Talos, he said. We need to return them. To the people who owned them.

Prutha looked at the dead priests. Pointed. *We found owners*, he said. *We give to them.*
